description.summary: Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine with native dense-vector, filtered kNN, lexical, semantic, and hybrid retrieval capabilities.
description.description: Elasticsearch stores JSON documents in distributed Lucene shards and combines mature lexical search, structured and geo filtering, dense-vector exact and approximate retrieval, quantized and disk-backed vector indexes, and hybrid fusion such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion. It can be self-managed or consumed through managed and serverless Elastic Cloud offerings. This record distinguishes vector-search support from dedicated vector-only databases and keeps version-, license-, deployment-, filter-, index-, and relevance-dependent behavior explicit.

indexingConsiderations: Select vector element type, dimensions, similarity, HNSW or disk-backed index options, and quantization only after measuring recall, latency, indexing cost, memory, and disk behavior.
Plan primary shard count, shard size, replica count, node roles, allocation awareness, and recovery capacity before large-scale ingestion.
Use index templates and explicit mappings to avoid accidental vector dimensions, analyzers, dynamic mappings, or field types.
Treat lexical analyzers, semantic models, vector indexes, and metadata fields as separate retrieval representations with explicit lifecycle and compatibility rules.
retrievalConsiderations: Place filters inside the kNN query when top-k filtered recall is required and distinguish them from post-filters.
Evaluate BM25-only, vector-only, semantic-only, and hybrid retrieval on the same relevance set before choosing RRF, linear fusion, boosts, or reranking.
Tune k, num_candidates, rank_window_size, rank_constant, filters, and candidate sizes under representative load.
Use profile, explain, slow logs, and retrieval metrics to separate query-planning, shard, model, and ranking costs.

limitations: Elasticsearch is a general search and analytics platform, so its operational and schema surface is broader than that of a dedicated vector database.
Approximate vector indexes and quantization trade exact recall for indexing speed, memory, disk, and query efficiency.
Pre-filter and post-filter placement changes top-k guarantees and can substantially affect latency and recall.
Shard count is an architectural decision: oversharding, undersharding, relocation, recovery, and hot shards can impair performance and resilience.
Search visibility is near-real-time and can lag acknowledged writes until refresh behavior makes new segments searchable.
RRF and other hybrid strategies depend on candidate windows, feature support, licensing, models, analyzers, and workload-specific relevance evaluation.
Elasticsearch does not provide general relational-style multi-document ACID transactions.
The default distribution and some capabilities are governed by Elastic licensing and deployment-specific subscription terms rather than by a single permissive product license.
usageGuidance: Record Elasticsearch, Lucene, client, and model versions because index defaults, vector formats, retrievers, APIs, and ranking behavior evolve across releases.
Benchmark the actual shard topology, vector dimensions, filters, query mix, candidate sizes, and hardware rather than relying on generic ANN results.
Use snapshots and restore drills as part of disaster recovery; replicas protect availability but do not replace backups.
Monitor shard health, refresh and merge pressure, indexing and search latency, cache behavior, disk watermarks, vector recall, and hybrid relevance in production.
Review feature availability and license requirements before depending on managed inference, advanced ranking, security, or serverless-specific behavior.

claims.statement: Elasticsearch stores dense vectors and supports exact vector scoring plus approximate k-nearest-neighbor retrieval with HNSW-based and disk-backed quantized index options across cosine, dot-product, Euclidean, maximum-inner-product, and bit-vector Hamming similarity behavior.
claims.rationale: The Elasticsearch reference identifies the product as a vector database and documents dense_vector storage, exact script_score retrieval, approximate kNN indexes, quantization, DiskBBQ, and supported vector similarities.

claims.statement: Elasticsearch supports metadata-aware approximate kNN retrieval with an explicit pre-filter applied during candidate collection, while filters outside the kNN filter parameter can act as post-filters and return fewer than the requested neighbors.

qualifiers.name: filterScope
qualifiers.value: Filter placement in the query DSL determines pre-filter versus post-filter behavior

claims.rationale: The kNN query documentation directly distinguishes pre-filtering inside the kNN query from post-filtering elsewhere in the query tree and describes their different top-k guarantees.

claims.statement: Elasticsearch combines lexical BM25 retrieval, dense-vector or semantic retrieval, filtering, and reranking through hybrid queries including Reciprocal Rank Fusion over multiple retrievers.

qualifiers.name: relevanceScope
qualifiers.value: Fusion strategy, candidate windows, boosts, models, and filters require workload-specific relevance evaluation

claims.rationale: Elastic documents hybrid lexical-vector search and the RRF retriever, including independent child retrievers, rank windows, rank constants, and final coordinating-node fusion.

claims.statement: Elasticsearch distributes indices into primary and replica shards across nodes, automatically balances shard copies, promotes replicas after primary failure, and supports self-managed, managed, and serverless deployment models.

qualifiers.name: deploymentScope
qualifiers.value: Shard topology is user-managed in self-hosted deployments and increasingly automated in managed and serverless offerings

claims.rationale: The distributed-architecture documentation describes indices as Lucene shards, primary and replica roles, allocation, balancing, failover, and deployment-dependent operational responsibility.

claims.statement: Elasticsearch uses primary-backup replication for document writes, provides document-level atomic operations rather than general multi-document ACID transactions, and supports off-cluster snapshots with lifecycle-managed backup and restore workflows.

qualifiers.name: durabilityScope
qualifiers.value: Acknowledgement, refresh visibility, replica health, snapshot repository configuration, and version compatibility affect durability and recovery behavior

claims.rationale: Elastic documents primary-stage validation and replication to in-sync replicas as well as snapshot repositories, automated snapshot lifecycle management, and restore constraints.

evidence.summary: Official Elastic sources describe Elasticsearch as a distributed search engine and vector database and document dense_vector exact and approximate search, HNSW, quantization, DiskBBQ, and vector similarity choices.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can classify Elasticsearch as a search engine with vector support rather than as a dedicated vector-only database.

sourceFragments.locator: Dense vector indexing, similarity, HNSW, quantization, and DiskBBQ sections

limitations: Official documentation establishes supported behavior but is not an independent performance benchmark.
Index defaults and available quantization options vary by vector element type and Elasticsearch version.

evidence.summary: The kNN query reference documents filter-aware approximate search and explicitly distinguishes candidate-stage pre-filters from query-tree post-filters.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark pre-filter support while warning that filter placement changes result-count and latency behavior.

sourceFragments.locator: filter parameter and pre-filters versus post-filters sections

limitations: Highly selective filters can increase graph traversal or trigger alternate search behavior, so workload testing remains necessary.
Post-filtering can return fewer than k documents even when enough matching documents exist in the index.

evidence.summary: Elastic documents BM25 lexical retrieval, dense or semantic retrieval, native filters, and RRF-based combination of multiple retriever result sets.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark built-in hybrid retrieval and RRF without treating any rank constant, candidate window, model, or weighting choice as universally optimal.

sourceFragments.locator: RRF retriever algorithm, child retrievers, and supported feature sections
Hybrid lexical, vector, filters, and reranking overview

limitations: RRF can truncate child results to the rank window and does not support every search feature in every combination.
Hybrid relevance depends on analyzers, embeddings, candidate sizes, fusion, boosts, filters, and evaluation data.

evidence.summary: Elastic documents primary and replica shards, automatic shard allocation and balancing, failover promotion, and different levels of infrastructure responsibility across deployment models.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark high horizontal scalability and replication support while retaining shard-sizing and operational complexity as explicit tradeoffs.

sourceFragments.locator: Clusters, nodes, primary shards, replicas, and serverless automation
Shard allocation, relocation, recovery, and primary promotion

limitations: Primary-shard count is fixed at index creation even though replica count can be changed later.
Oversharding, undersharding, relocation, recovery, and hot spots can materially affect cost and performance.

evidence.summary: Elastic documents primary-backup write replication to in-sync copies and snapshot repositories for backup, migration, and disaster recovery.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark configurable consistency, document-level atomicity, replication, and strong backup capabilities without claiming relational multi-document transactions.

sourceFragments.locator: Primary, replica, in-sync copy, acknowledgement, and failure-handling model
Snapshot repositories, lifecycle management, backup, and restore workflows

limitations: Search visibility is near-real-time and depends on refresh behavior rather than only on write acknowledgement.
Snapshot restore depends on repository availability, version compatibility, cluster state, index state, and sufficient capacity.
